nameStory: This tiny freshwater creature is named after Polyphemus, the giant one-eyed cyclops from Greek mythology. The name perfectly captures its most striking feature - a single, prominent black eye that dominates its transparent body like the cyclops's legendary eye.
description: Polyphemus pediculus is a microscopic water flea that lives in freshwater lakes and ponds throughout New England. Despite being called a water flea, it's actually a tiny crustacean related to shrimp and crabs, not an insect at all. This translucent creature is barely visible to the naked eye, measuring less than 2 millimeters long. Its body is nearly transparent with a distinctive single large black eye that makes it unmistakable under a microscope or magnifying glass.

idTips.label: Single Black Eye
idTips.description: One prominent black compound eye dominates the front of its transparent body - this is the most reliable way to identify it

idTips.label: Transparent Body
idTips.description: The body is crystal clear like glass, allowing you to see internal organs and structures through its shell

idTips.label: Swimming Style
idTips.description: Moves through water with jerky, hopping motions rather than smooth gliding, using its large antennae like oars

idTips.label: Rounded Shape
idTips.description: Has a compact, oval-shaped body enclosed in a transparent shell that looks like a tiny bubble

idTips.label: Antenna Movement
idTips.description: Two large, branched antennae constantly beat back and forth, creating small currents in the water

habitat: Found in the open water of freshwater lakes, ponds, and slow-moving rivers throughout New England. They prefer the deeper, cooler waters away from shore where they can swim freely in the water column. You'll need to collect a water sample and examine it under magnification to spot these tiny creatures.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to increase as water temperatures warm, making this a good time to find them in shallow areas that are warming up first.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when they're most active and easiest to spot in water samples.
seasonality.fall: Still present but populations may start to decline as temperatures drop, though they can remain active in deeper waters.
seasonality.winter: Present year-round under ice cover, though less active and harder to find in the coldest months.

funFact: Despite having only one eye, Polyphemus can detect colors and navigate complex underwater environments better than many creatures with two eyes - its single compound eye contains hundreds of individual light sensors that create a detailed mosaic view of its watery world.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other water fleas like Daphnia, but remember the eye rule - Daphnia has a small, less prominent eye, while Polyphemus has one giant black eye that's impossible to miss. Think 'Polyphemus = one giant eye like the mythical cyclops.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'water flea,' this creature is not related to the fleas that bite mammals. The name comes from their small size and jerky swimming movements that reminded early naturalists of jumping fleas. They're actually more closely related to lobsters and crabs than to any insect.
compareHints: Polyphemus is the only member of its genus found in New England waters, making identification straightforward once you spot that characteristic single large eye. Compared to other water fleas in the region, it's distinguished by having just one prominent black eye rather than the smaller, paired eyes found in most other freshwater crustaceans. Its transparent body and distinctive hopping swimming style also set it apart from similar-sized aquatic creatures.
